pages.text:
*The Owl Alley Sheet, No. 3. Today's news: one hundred years of soot came down.*

The brooms were made of dried bamboo, stiff and scratching. They hissed against the wooden floors. Today the whole house turned inside out.

Haru’s job was the most dangerous task in the shop: cleaning the block shelves. She had to wipe the dust from the cherry wood without touching a single carved face. One slip, one smudge, and a week of work would be lost.

Outside, the alley shook with laughter. Neighbors held a large, flour-dusted helper. They roared. They tossed him into the air. A cloud of white powder puffed around his head. He landed on a pile of mats, coughing and grinning.

"Look at him," Kichi laughed, wiping flour from his nose. "He looks like a snowman that lost its carrot."

Rice cakes were passed around, warm and slightly sticky. Haru bit into one. Sweet bean paste filled her mouth. The shop was bright. Dust motes danced in the light. The air smelled of clean wood and fresh rice.
pages.image: Haru, in a rust-orange kimono and indigo apron, carefully wipes dust from wooden printing blocks on a high shelf, while outside in a bright alley, neighbors in quilted coats cheerfully toss a flour-dusted helper into the air.

pages.text:
The well at the end of Owl Alley was the heart of the street. By midday, half the neighborhood stood there. Buckets clanked. Voices rose and fell in the cold air.

Okiku, the noodle maker, tied a white towel around her grey hair. She laughed at a story about a cat. Umekichi, the tofu maker, leaned on his wife Osen’s arm. His huge forearms rested on the stone rim. He was broad and cheerful, his white apron already stained with bean pulp.

From the bathhouse came Hachi, the owner. He had thick eyebrows and a loud voice. He carried a towel over his shoulder. He looked as if he had just finished arguing with the wind itself. Beside him stood Shin, the furnace boy.

Shin was small. Soot-streaked. He yawned so wide it seemed his jaw might unhinge.

"Sleepyhead," Hachi said. But gently.

Shin yawned again. He rubbed his eyes with black fingers. The sun was warm on their faces. Haru listened. Her booklet hung at her belt. The street was a web of voices, smells, and lives intertwined.
pages.image: At a stone well in a narrow wooden alley in bright winter sun, Okiku in a faded pink quilted jacket with a white towel on her grey hair, Umekichi in a white work shirt and long white apron, Hachi in a dark navy short coat with a towel over his shoulder, Haru in her rust-orange kimono, and small skinny Shin, a nine-year-old boy in a soot-grey jacket yawning widely with a soot-smudged face, stand close together.

pages.text:
Haru sat on the bathhouse steps, her brush tapping her teeth. She was listening.

The conversation shifted. Okiku was not there, but her name was. A woman with a sharp voice leaned toward another. "Did you taste the soba this week? It was grey. Not the nice, pale color."

The second woman nodded slowly. "My cousin said the same. She said it was rough. Like sand in the flour."

A third voice, low and cautious, added, "They say she mixes it with something else. Something cheaper. To save money."

Haru’s hand moved to her booklet. She wrote the words down quickly. *Soba is grey. Rough. Mixed with sand.* Then she paused. Her brush hovered.

None of them had said they had seen it. None of them had said they had tasted it themselves. They were repeating what they had heard. The words felt thin in her hand, like wet paper that might tear. She crossed out the sentence. The ink bled slightly into the fiber.
pages.image: Haru sits on stone bathhouse steps, holding a small paper booklet, her face serious and thoughtful, while two women in quilted coats whisper close together in the background near a wooden door.

pages.text:
Back in the shop, the smell of ink was sharp and clean. Father Sota sat at the carving table, his knife still in his hand. He did not look up when Haru entered.

"I heard a rumor," Haru said, placing the booklet on the table. "About Okiku’s noodles."

Father Sota set his knife down. He wiped his hands on his dark brown coat. "Three questions, Haru. Did you see it with your own eyes?"

Haru shook her head. "No."

"Who said it first?"

"I don't know. Several people said the same thing."

"And what does the person gain by saying it?"

Haru frowned. She had not thought of that. "Nothing?"

Father Sota picked up a small block of wood. "If you want to write about noodles, Haru, go and watch noodles. Not the talk. The work." He pointed to the door. "The truth is not in the air. It is in the hands that make the thing."
pages.image: Father Sota, a broad man in a dark brown work coat and white headband, sits at a low wooden table holding a small carved block, looking calmly at Haru, who stands holding her paper booklet with a worried expression.

pages.text:
Dusk turned the alley purple and orange. Haru walked to the canal end, where the air tasted of woodsmoke and boiling water.

Okiku’s stall glowed under a single lantern. The broth hissed and steamed in thick white clouds, curling up into the cold. Okiku stood by the pot, her back to the street. She hummed a low, steady tune. Her hands moved with the rhythm of years.

Haru stood at the edge of the crowd. Her booklet hung heavy at her belt. It felt like a stone. The women whispered around her, their voices soft and sharp. Haru had no questions for them. She had a question for the woman who worked.

She took a slow breath. The cold bit her lungs. Then she stepped forward, her straw sandals clicking on the wet stone.

"Okiku-san," she said. Her voice was steady, though her heart beat like a drum in a festival. "May I watch you make them?"

Okiku turned. Her face was unreadable. She looked at Haru’s ink-stained fingers. Then she looked at her eyes. The steam rose between them, blurring the world for a moment, like a breath on a cold mirror.
pages.image: Haru stands in front of a small noodle stall at dusk, looking up at Okiku, a round woman in a faded pink jacket who turns from a steaming pot, the lantern light glowing warm against the dark blue evening sky.
